bio_ocrb.1.15.summary: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced from a single clone of hybridoma cells, specifically designed to bind to targeted antigens on cancer cells. In cancer treatment, they can be used alone to trigger the immune system, carry radioactive substances or toxic drugs directly to tumours, or block receptor sites to stop cells from dividing. Because they target specific cancer antigens while leaving healthy cells largely unharmed, they provide a much more precise treatment alternative than traditional chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

core.p: Monoclonal antibodies (often abbreviated as mAbs) are artificial, **identical copies** of a single type of antibody. Because they are derived from a single clone of cells, every single molecule is identical and engineered to bind to one specific target structure.
bullets: Produced in a laboratory setting for medical treatments and diagnostic tests.
Targeted to bind to **one specific antigen** with absolute precision.
Can be designed to recognise unique proteins found exclusively on the surface of cancer cells.
Formed by fusing mouse B-lymphocytes with myeloma (tumour) cells to create hybridomas.

callouts.p: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced from a single clone of cells, designed to target and bind to one specific antigen.

fig.cap: Figure 1: Structure of a monoclonal antibody showing identical binding sites designed to lock onto specific target antigens on cancer cell surfaces.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><path d="M170,160 L170,110 L200,90 L230,110 L230,160" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M200,90 L200,50" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="200" cy="45" r="12" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M155,100 L170,110" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M245,100 L230,110" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><text x="165" y="190" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Constant Region</text><text x="165" y="35" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Binding Site</text><text x="50" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Identical Y-shape structure</text></svg>

core.p: Monoclonal antibodies can attach directly to specific receptors or antigens on the surface of cancer cells. Once bound, they can disrupt cancer cell function or mark the cell out for destruction by the body's own immune system.
bullets: Binding to antigens can physically block chemical signals that stimulate uncontrolled cell division.
They can act as a **flag or marker**, making cancer cells easily identifiable to phagocytes and killer T-cells.
Triggers the body's natural immune response to attack and destroy the tagged tumour cell.
Helps to slow down or completely halt tumour growth in specific types of cancer like breast cancer.

callouts.p: Unconjugated monoclonal antibodies bind to cancer antigens to trigger immune destruction or block growth factors without carrying extra drugs.

core.p: Instead of relying solely on the immune system, monoclonal antibodies can be chemically linked to powerful toxic drugs, radioactive isotopes, or chemicals. This creates a targeted delivery vehicle known as an **antibody-drug conjugate**.
bullets: The monoclonal antibody acts as a homing device, seeking out and binding only to cancer cell antigens.
The attached **toxic drug or radioactive substance** is delivered directly to the tumour site.
Minimizes damage to healthy, non-cancerous tissues throughout the rest of the patient's body.
Reduces the severe side effects typically associated with conventional, untargeted chemotherapy.

callouts.p: A monoclonal antibody chemically bonded to a toxin or radioactive isotope to deliver lethal treatments directly to cancer cells.

fig.cap: Figure 2: An antibody-drug conjugate binding to a cancer cell antigen, releasing a toxic payload directly inside the targeted tumour.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f0fdf4"/><circle cx="280" cy="140" r="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="280" cy="100" r="6" fill="#ef4444"/><path d="M120,140 L170,140 L200,120" fill="none" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="200" cy="120" r="8" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="70" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Monoclonal Antibody</text><text x="240" y="190" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Cancer Cell</text><text x="170" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#1e293b">Toxic Payload</text></svg>

core.p: Many cancer cells rely on specific growth factor signals to multiply rapidly. Monoclonal antibodies can be engineered to bind to these growth factor receptors on the cancer cell membrane, **blocking them** so signals cannot get through.
bullets: Prevents hormones or growth factors from binding to their target receptors on the cancer cell.
Cuts off the chemical instructions telling the cancer cell to grow and divide.
Induces **apoptosis** (programmed cell death) in cancer cells that are starved of growth signals.
Particularly useful in treating hormone-driven cancers such as certain forms of breast cancer.

callouts.p: Always state that monoclonal antibodies bind to *specific* antigens, not just 'cells', to secure full marks in mechanism questions.

core.p: Traditional cancer treatments like chemotherapy and radiotherapy are non-selective, damaging both cancerous and healthy rapidly-dividing cells (like hair follicles and gut lining). Monoclonal antibodies offer significant advantages in precision.
bullets: Highly specific: they target only cells carrying the specific antigen, sparing healthy tissues.
Lower incidence of systemic side effects such as severe hair loss, nausea, and immune suppression.
Can combine multiple therapeutic approaches, such as immune stimulation and drug delivery simultaneously.
Improves patient quality of life during the course of treatment.

core.p: Despite their high precision, monoclonal antibodies are not without drawbacks. Early clinical use revealed significant challenges that researchers have had to work hard to overcome.
bullets: Originally derived from mouse cells, human immune systems often recognized them as foreign and **created an immune response** against them.
Can cause severe, unexpected side effects and allergic reactions (infusion reactions).
Production process is complex, time-consuming, and **very expensive**, limiting widespread availability.
Cancer cells can sometimes mutate and alter their surface antigens, making the antibodies ineffective.

callouts.p: Students often think monoclonal antibodies have zero side effects because they are targeted. They still cause immune reactions and toxicity.

core.p: To understand how they treat cancer, recall how monoclonal antibodies are made using hybridoma technology. A mouse is vaccinated to stimulate the production of specific antibodies, and its spleen cells are harvested.
bullets: Mouse B-lymphocytes (which produce the required antibody) cannot divide continuously in culture.
Myeloma cells (tumour cells) can divide endlessly but do not produce the desired antibodies.
B-lymphocytes are fused with myeloma cells using **polyethylene glycol (PEG)** to form hybridoma cells.
Hybridomas share both properties: they produce specific antibodies *and* divide indefinitely.

callouts.p: A hybrid cell created by fusing a specific B-lymphocyte with a myeloma tumour cell, capable of producing identical antibodies indefinitely.

fig.cap: Figure 3: Hybridoma production: fusing a mouse B-lymphocyte with a myeloma cell to create a dividing hybridoma clone.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#fef3c7"/><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="30" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="2"/><text x="75" y="105" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">B-cell</text><circle cx="220" cy="100" r="30" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="195" y="105" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Myeloma</text><path d="M140,100 L180,100" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><circle cx="320" cy="100" r="35" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#6b21a8" stroke-width="2"/><text x="295" y="105" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Hybridoma</text><path d="M260,100 L280,100" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

core.p: Once hybridomas are formed, single cells are isolated and allowed to multiply to produce identical copies that secrete the exact desired antibody.
bullets: Hybridomas are grown in a selective growth medium (HAT medium) where only fused hybrid cells survive.
Individual hybridoma cells are separated and screened to ensure they produce the correct antibody.
Selected hybridomas are cultured on a large scale in industrial fermenters.
The antibodies are then **extracted, purified, and bottled** for medical use.

core.p: To overcome the problem of human immune rejection of mouse antibodies, modern genetic engineering techniques have allowed scientists to produce humanised monoclonal antibodies.
bullets: **Chimeric antibodies**: Combine mouse variable regions (which bind the antigen) with human constant regions.
**Humanised antibodies**: Only the tiny complementary-determining regions (antigen-binding loops) are from mice; the rest of the antibody molecule is completely human.
Significantly reduces the patient's immune system attacking the treatment as a foreign invader.
Increases the persistence and effectiveness of the antibody in human patients.

callouts.p: Engineered antibodies with mostly human protein sequences to prevent human immune rejection.

core.p: Several monoclonal antibody therapies are now standard treatments approved for NHS and global clinical use against specific cancers.
bullets: **Trastuzumab (Herceptin)**: Used to treat HER2-positive breast cancer by blocking growth factor receptors.
**Rituximab**: Used for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, binding to CD20 antigens on B-cells to trigger destruction.
**Bevacizumab**: Targets vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to cut off blood supply to tumours (anti-angiogenesis).
Ongoing clinical trials continue to test new antibody combinations for hard-to-treat solid tumours.

analogy.p: Monoclonal antibodies act like heat-seeking missiles programmed to lock onto a specific signature (the antigen) on an enemy tank (the cancer cell). Once they lock on, they can either explode immediately (delivering a toxic drug payload) or call in an airstrike (alerting white blood cells to destroy the target). Where this analogy breaks down is that missiles destroy themselves upon impact, whereas antibodies bind to antigens without being consumed in the initial binding action.

terms.d: An identical antibody produced from a single clone of hybridoma cells, specific to one antigen.
A fusion of a mouse B-lymphocyte and a myeloma cell used to produce monoclonal antibodies.
A protein marker on the surface of a cell that triggers an immune response.
A type of tumour cell used in hybridoma production because it divides indefinitely.
A monoclonal antibody chemically linked to a toxic drug or radioactive isotope for targeted cancer treatment.
An antibody engineered to have mostly human sequences with only mouse antigen-binding tips, reducing immune rejection.
Programmed cell death induced in damaged or abnormal cells.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
A receptor protein overexpressed in certain aggressive forms of breast cancer, targeted by Herceptin.
Untargeted medicine used to kill rapidly dividing cells throughout the body.
A protein molecule on a cell membrane that receives chemical signals.
A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division.

mistakes.w: Saying monoclonal antibodies kill cells by themselves without specifying antigens.
mistakes.r: They must bind to specific antigens on the surface of cancer cells.

mistakes.w: Believing monoclonal antibodies are made directly from human white blood cells.
mistakes.r: They are made using hybridomas formed from mouse B-lymphocytes fused with tumour cells.

mistakes.w: Stating that monoclonal antibodies cause no side effects.
mistakes.r: They can cause significant side effects including fever, allergic reactions, and immune responses against mouse proteins.

mistakes.w: Confusing antigens with antibodies.
mistakes.r: Antigens are markers on cells; antibodies are proteins produced by white blood cells that bind to antigens.

mistakes.w: Thinking chemotherapy and monoclonal antibodies are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Chemotherapy is non-specific and kills all dividing cells, whereas monoclonal antibodies target specific antigens.

mistakes.w: Describing hybridomas as normal cells.
mistakes.r: Hybridomas are artificial fused cells combining antibody production and continuous division.

mistakes.w: Writing that antibodies enter the cancer cell nucleus to work.
mistakes.r: Monoclonal antibodies bind to external cell surface antigens or receptors.

exam.q: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer.
model: Monoclonal antibodies are designed to bind to specific antigens on cancer cells.
They can trigger the patient's immune system to attack and destroy the cancer cells.
They can be bound to a toxic drug or radioactive substance to deliver treatment directly to the tumour.
This minimizes damage to healthy, non-cancerous body tissues.
They can also block receptor sites on cancer cells to stop them dividing and growing.
An example includes Herceptin used for breast cancer.
exam.tip: Cover both direct immune triggering and drug delivery to secure all 6 marks.

exam.q: What is a hybridoma cell?
model: A cell formed by fusing a B-lymphocyte with a tumour (myeloma) cell.
It can produce specific antibodies and divide continuously.
exam.tip: Mention both fusion sources and the dual capability for both marks.

exam.q: Give one advantage of using monoclonal antibodies instead of traditional chemotherapy for cancer treatment.
model: They target specific cancer cells / cause fewer side effects to healthy tissues.
exam.tip: Keep it concise and focus on specificity.

exam.q: Explain why early monoclonal antibody treatments caused severe side effects in human patients.
model: The antibodies were originally derived from mouse cells.
The human immune system recognized them as foreign and triggered an immune response against them.
exam.tip: Always link early side effects to mouse proteins being recognised as foreign.

exam.q: Describe how an antibody-drug conjugate works to treat a tumour.
model: The monoclonal antibody binds specifically to antigens on the cancer cell.
It acts as a carrier to deliver a toxic drug directly to the tumour site.
This kills the cancer cell while reducing damage to healthy tissues.
exam.tip: Mention the specific binding followed by localized toxic delivery.

exam.q: Name the cell type fused with a B-lymphocyte to create a hybridoma.
model: Myeloma cell / tumour cell.
exam.tip: Single mark question; ensure exact terminology is used.

exam.q: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can stop cancer cells from multiplying without using toxic drugs.
model: Antibodies can bind to growth factor receptors on the cancer cell membrane.
This blocks chemical signals required for cell division.
Without these growth signals, the cancer cells stop dividing or undergo apoptosis.
exam.tip: Focus on receptor blocking and signaling interruption.

exam.q: Suggest why monoclonal antibody therapy can become ineffective if a patient's cancer mutates.
model: Mutation changes the structure of the antigens on the cancer cell surface.
The monoclonal antibody can no longer bind to the altered antigen.
exam.tip: Link mutation directly to a change in antigen shape preventing binding.

exam.q: What is the role of the variable region on a monoclonal antibody?
model: It provides the specific binding site.
It is complementary in shape to one specific antigen.
exam.tip: Use the keyword 'complementary' for maximum marks.

worked.q: A pharmaceutical company produces a batch of monoclonal antibodies. Out of 5000 hybridoma cells cultured, 12% successfully produce the desired antibody for a cancer treatment. Calculate how many hybridoma cells produce the correct antibody.
steps: Identify the total number of hybridoma cells: 5000.
Identify the percentage producing the desired antibody: 12%.

worked.q: In a clinical trial, 450 cancer patients receive a new monoclonal antibody treatment. 68% of patients experience reduced tumour size, 22% show stable condition, and the rest experience tumour growth. Calculate the number of patients who experienced tumour growth.
steps: Find the total percentage of patients with reduced or stable conditions: 68% + 22% = 90%.
Calculate the percentage experiencing tumour growth: 100% - 90% = 10%.
Calculate the number of patients: 10% of 450 = (10 / 100) x 450 = 45.

bio_ocrb.1.1.summary: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protists that can be transmitted between individuals. In humans, these range from viral infections like HIV and influenza to fungal issues like athlete's foot and protist-borne malaria. Plants are also susceptible to specific pathogens such as TMV and crown gall, which disrupt physiological processes like photosynthesis and nutrient transport, leading to reduced growth and crop yield.

core.p: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious (communicable) disease. To achieve a grade 9, you must distinguish between the four main types based on their structure and how they damage the host.
bullets: **Viruses**: Non-living genetic material (DNA/RNA) wrapped in protein; they must hijack host cells to replicate.
**Bacteria**: Prokaryotic cells that release **toxins** or damage cells directly.
**Fungi**: Eukaryotic organisms (multicellular or unicellular) that use hyphae to penetrate surfaces.
**Protists**: Single-celled eukaryotes, often transferred via a **vector**.

core.p: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that targets the human immune system, specifically **lymphocytes** (white blood cells).
bullets: **Transmission**: Spread through direct contact with infected body fluids (blood, semen, breast milk) or sharing needles.
**Mechanism**: The virus enters lymphocytes and uses their machinery to replicate, eventually destroying the cells.
**Progression**: Initially causes flu-like symptoms. If untreated, it leads to **AIDS** (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome).
**Impact**: The immune system becomes so weak it cannot fight off 'opportunistic' infections or cancers.

callouts.p: HIV is the pathogen (the virus); AIDS is the condition (the late-stage failure of the immune system).

core.p: Influenza, commonly known as the flu, is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by the influenza virus.
bullets: **Transmission**: Airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing (droplet infection).
**Symptoms**: High fever, body aches, fatigue, and sore throat.
**Prevention**: Annual vaccinations (due to rapid mutation of the virus) and good hygiene (Catch it, Bin it, Kill it).

core.p: Salmonella bacteria cause food poisoning, typically through the ingestion of contaminated food prepared in unhygienic conditions.
bullets: **Transmission**: Eating undercooked poultry, eggs, or food contaminated by cross-infection from raw meat.
**Symptoms**: Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting, and diarrhoea caused by **bacterial toxins**.
**Control**: In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against Salmonella to limit the spread to humans.

core.p: Malaria is caused by a protist called *Plasmodium*. It has a complex life cycle involving both a human host and an insect vector.
bullets: **Vector**: The female **Anopheles mosquito**; it picks up the protist when feeding on an infected person and passes it to the next.
**Symptoms**: Recurrent episodes of severe fever and shaking, which can be fatal.
**Prevention**: Breaking the life cycle by using mosquito nets, insect repellent, or draining stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.

core.p: A common fungal infection of the skin, usually between the toes, caused by various types of fungi.
bullets: **Transmission**: Direct contact with infected skin or indirect contact via contaminated surfaces (e.g., gym floors, towels).
**Symptoms**: Itchy, red, flaky, or cracked skin.
**Environment**: Fungi thrive in warm, damp conditions, which is why sweaty shoes are a major risk factor.

core.p: TMV is a widespread plant pathogen affecting many species, including tomatoes and tobacco plants.
bullets: **Symptoms**: A distinctive 'mosaic' pattern of discolouration on the leaves.
**Impact**: The discolouration means less **chlorophyll** is present in the leaves.
**Result**: Reduced photosynthesis leads to less glucose production, which stunts the plant's growth.

callouts.p: Always link leaf damage to reduced photosynthesis and then to reduced growth for full marks in plant disease questions.

core.p: Also known as Chalara, this is a fungal disease affecting ash trees.
bullets: **Pathogen**: The fungus *Hymenoscyphus fraxineus*.
**Symptoms**: Leaf loss (defoliation) and dark brown/black lesions (cankers) on the bark.
**Transmission**: Fungal spores are carried through the air by the wind.
**Impact**: Often fatal to the tree as it weakens the vascular system.

core.p: Caused by the bacterium *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*, which infects many species of dicotyledonous plants.
bullets: **Mechanism**: The bacteria insert a specific piece of DNA (from a **plasmid**) into the plant's genome.
**Symptoms**: Large, tumor-like growths called **galls** appear on the roots or stem.
**Impact**: The galls encircle the stem or root, cutting off the flow of water (xylem) and nutrients (phloem), which can kill the plant.

analogy.p: Think of the body or a plant as a castle. Viruses are like spies who sneak in and take over the castle's own workshops to build more spies. Bacteria are like an invading army that sets up camp and releases poison (toxins) into the water supply. Fungi are like mold growing on the walls, slowly digesting the stone. Malaria is like a Trojan horse, where a mosquito (the horse) carries the soldiers (protists) inside. The analogy breaks down because, unlike a castle, biological organisms have active immune systems that can learn and adapt to specific invaders.

terms.d: A microorganism that causes infectious disease.
An organism (like a mosquito) that carries a pathogen from one host to another without being infected itself.
A poisonous substance produced by bacteria that damages cells and tissues.
A diverse group of eukaryotic microorganisms, some of which are parasitic.
Thread-like structures of a fungus that can penetrate skin or plant surfaces.
The yellowing of plant leaves due to lack of chlorophyll, often caused by TMV.
A small loop of DNA in bacteria; used by Agrobacterium to transfer genes into plants.
A disease that can be spread from one person or organism to another.
A type of white blood cell targeted by the HIV virus.
A localized area of diseased tissue on a plant, often seen in Ash Dieback.
A pattern of spots or light and dark green patches on plant leaves.
The bursting of a cell, often the final stage of viral replication.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics can be used to treat the flu or HIV.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics only kill bacteria; they have no effect on viruses.

mistakes.w: The mosquito causes malaria.
mistakes.r: The mosquito is the vector; the Plasmodium protist is the pathogen.

mistakes.w: HIV and AIDS are the same thing.
mistakes.r: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the late-stage syndrome resulting from HIV infection.

mistakes.w: TMV kills plants by eating the leaves.
mistakes.r: TMV causes discolouration which reduces photosynthesis, leading to stunted growth.

mistakes.w: Salmonella is caused by a virus in chicken.
mistakes.r: Salmonella is a bacterium.

mistakes.w: Crown gall is a type of plant cancer.
mistakes.r: While it involves uncontrolled cell growth (tumors), it is caused by bacterial DNA insertion, not spontaneous mutation.

mistakes.w: Ash dieback is spread by insects.
mistakes.r: Ash dieback is primarily spread by wind-blown fungal spores.

exam.q: Explain why plants infected with Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) often have stunted growth.
model: TMV causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves.
This results in a loss of chlorophyll in the affected areas.
Less light is absorbed, so the rate of photosynthesis is reduced.
Less glucose is produced for respiration/protein synthesis, leading to less growth.
exam.tip: Always follow the logic: Leaf damage -> Chlorophyll -> Photosynthesis -> Glucose -> Growth.

exam.q: Identify the type of pathogen that causes Malaria and the organism that acts as its vector.
model: Pathogen: Protist (or Plasmodium).
Vector: (Female Anopheles) Mosquito.
exam.tip: Be specific about the vector; 'insect' is usually too vague for full marks.

exam.q: Describe two ways the spread of Malaria can be reduced.
model: Use of mosquito nets to prevent bites.
Draining stagnant water to prevent mosquitoes from breeding.
exam.tip: Focus on 'breaking the life cycle' of the vector.

exam.q: State the method of transmission for the HIV virus.
model: Exchange of body fluids (e.g., blood, sexual contact, or needle sharing).
exam.tip: Do not just say 'contact'; it must be fluid exchange.

exam.q: How does the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens cause galls in plants?
model: It inserts a plasmid/DNA into the plant's cells.
This causes the plant cells to grow and divide uncontrollably.
exam.tip: Mentioning the 'plasmid' is key for higher-tier marks.

exam.q: Explain why a person with AIDS is more likely to die from a common cold than a healthy person.
model: HIV destroys the white blood cells/lymphocytes.
The immune system is severely weakened/compromised.
The body cannot produce enough antibodies to fight off even mild infections.
exam.tip: Link the destruction of specific cells to the overall failure of the immune response.

exam.q: Compare the transmission of Influenza and Salmonella.
model: Influenza is airborne/spread via droplets.
Salmonella is foodborne/spread via contaminated food/ingestion.
exam.tip: Use comparative language like 'whereas' or 'on the other hand'.

exam.q: Describe the symptoms of Ash Dieback.
model: Black/brown lesions on the bark (cankers).
Dieback of leaves/shoots or defoliation.
exam.tip: Remember 'Chalara' is the old name for the same disease.

exam.q: Which pathogen causes Athlete's Foot?
model: Fungus (or Fungi).
exam.tip: Simple recall question; don't overthink it.

worked.q: A farmer notices a large growth on the stem of a rose bush. Identify the likely disease and explain how it affects the plant's transport systems.
steps: Identify the symptom: A large growth (tumor) on the stem is a 'gall'.
Identify the disease: Crown Gall caused by Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
Explain the transport impact: The gall grows around the stem, compressing the vascular bundles.
Link to specific tissues: Xylem (water) and Phloem (sugars) transport is restricted.
worked.ans: The disease is Crown Gall. The bacterial infection causes a tumor (gall) to grow on the stem. This growth physically blocks or restricts the xylem and phloem vessels, preventing the movement of water to leaves and sugars to roots, eventually killing the plant.

worked.q: A student is comparing HIV and Influenza. List three differences in their transmission or effect on the body.
steps: Think about transmission: HIV (fluids) vs Flu (air).
Think about symptoms: HIV (long-term immune failure) vs Flu (short-term fever/aches).
Think about treatment/prevention: HIV (antiretrovirals) vs Flu (annual vaccine).
worked.ans: 1. HIV is transmitted via body fluids, whereas Influenza is spread through airborne droplets. 2. HIV specifically attacks the immune system (lymphocytes), while Influenza primarily affects the respiratory system. 3. HIV is a chronic, long-term infection that can lead to AIDS, while Influenza is usually an acute, short-term illness.
